title: Exile, Persia and the Second Temple
bigQuestion: How did a people keep its story and its identity after losing its land, its king and its Temple?

story.title: A Clay Cylinder in a Glass Case
story.kicker: In 1879 a digger working for the British Museum pulled a barrel of baked clay from the ruins of Babylon.
paragraphs: Hormuzd Rassam grew up in Mosul, in what is now Iraq, and spent his life digging for the British Museum. In March 1879 his workers were clearing a temple wall in the ruins of Babylon. They found a clay object shaped like a small barrel, about nine inches long, covered in tiny wedge-shaped marks. It was broken but mostly whole. Rassam packed it and shipped it to London.

The marks were cuneiform, the script of ancient Mesopotamia. When scholars read them, they found the voice of a king. The cylinder was made for Cyrus, ruler of Persia, soon after his army took Babylon in 539 BCE. In it Cyrus says that Babylon's own god, Marduk, chose him to rule. He says he entered the city in peace and let captive peoples and their gods go home to their shrines.

The cylinder never mentions Judah, Jerusalem, or the exiles from the kingdom of Judah. But the book of Ezra opens with a decree from this same Cyrus. Ezra 1 says he told the exiles to go up to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of their God. Readers have set the clay and the scroll side by side ever since. The stone shows a policy; the book shows what one people said that policy meant for them.

Today the Cyrus Cylinder sits in a glass case in the British Museum. It has traveled to Tehran, to Washington, and in 2013 to five American cities. Some call it the first charter of human rights, though most historians say that goes too far. It is a king's announcement, written to make Babylon's priests accept a new ruler.

This chapter begins with a people carried off to Babylon and ends with the world Jesus was born into, about five centuries later. Between those points, the Bible's own books changed shape. Stories were written down and gathered. Prayer found a home outside the Temple. And a small province under one empire after another decided what it would keep.
story.think: Cyrus's cylinder never names the exiles from Judah, but Ezra says Cyrus sent them home. How can both be true?

lessons.title: Carried Off to Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Babylon deported Judah's leaders in 597 and 586 BCE, and the exiles settled in villages where they could keep together.
reading: The word *exile* means being forced to live away from your homeland. Babylon carried off the people of Judah in stages. In 597 BCE King Jehoiachin, his court, craftsmen and soldiers were taken. The text says thousands went (2 Kings 24:14). In 586 BCE, after the Temple burned, more were deported. Only the poorest were left to work the land (2 Kings 25:12). Some others fled to Egypt, taking the prophet Jeremiah with them.

Unlike Assyria, Babylon did not scatter the exiles. It settled them in groups. The prophet Ezekiel lived among exiles at a place called Tel Abib by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 3:15). Clay business records found in Iraq name a village the Babylonians called the town of Judah. They show Judeans farming, paying taxes and using names built on their God's name, decades after the fall.

The exiles' feelings survive in their poems. Psalm 137 pictures captives sitting by Babylon's rivers, hanging up their harps, unable to sing when their captors ask for a song. The book of Lamentations mourns Jerusalem in five poems. Jewish communities still read Lamentations each year on the fast of Tisha B'Av, which remembers the Temple's destruction.

Historians call these years the *Babylonian exile*, from 586 to 538 BCE. The number of people involved was small, perhaps tens of thousands. Their effect was large. Many scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible was gathered, edited or written in this period and the one that followed, by people asking why the disaster happened and what came next.

words.d: being forced to live away from your homeland; here, the Judeans' years in Babylon
the period from 586 to 538 BCE when many of Judah's people lived as captives in Babylon
a book of five poems mourning the fall of Jerusalem, read by Jews each year on Tisha B'Av

look.title: A song from the exile
look.text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
look.prompt: The psalm names a place, an action and a memory. Which word carries the most feeling for you, and why?

check.q: What does exile mean?
choices: Being forced to live away from your homeland
Being sent to fight a war
check.why: The exiles of Judah were forced to live in Babylon, far from Jerusalem.

check.q: How did Babylon's treatment of the exiles differ from Assyria's?
choices: Babylon settled the exiles in groups instead of scattering them
Babylon sent the exiles to Egypt
Babylon let the exiles return at once
check.why: Ezekiel lived among exiles at Tel Abib, and records name a town of Judah in Babylonia. Assyria had spread Israel's people across its empire.

check.q: Which book do Jewish communities read on Tisha B'Av to remember the Temple's fall?
check.why: Lamentations is five poems mourning Jerusalem. Esther is read at Purim.

lessons.title: What the Exile Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Without land, king or Temple, the exiles held on through text, prayer and practices that marked them as a people.
reading: Before 586 BCE, religion in Judah centered on the Temple. Priests offered sacrifices there, and pilgrims came for festivals. In Babylon there was no Temple, and the law did not allow building another one elsewhere. The exiles needed a way to be faithful without an altar. The answers they found shaped Judaism and, later, Christianity and Islam.

One answer was the written word. Many scholars think the exile is when the *Torah*, the five books of Moses, took something close to its final form, along with the story from Joshua to Kings. The prophets' words were collected into books. A people that could not gather at a building could gather around a scroll. The Hebrew word for this kind of study and reading, and for the book itself, would later be central to Jewish life.

Another answer was practice. The *Sabbath*, the weekly day of rest, could be kept anywhere. So could circumcision and the food laws. In a foreign land these marked who belonged. Many scholars also place the roots of the *synagogue*, a house of prayer and study, in these years, though the oldest clear evidence for synagogue buildings comes centuries later.

Prophets living among the exiles gave the third answer: hope. Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones that stand up and live again. The text says this means the house of Israel will return (Ezekiel 37). Isaiah 40 opens with the words Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Many scholars think the chapters from Isaiah 40 onward were written in the exile. Jewish and Christian readers alike have turned to them in hard times.

words.d: the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy; the word also means teaching
the seventh day of the week, kept as a day of rest; in Hebrew, Shabbat
a Jewish house of prayer and study; many scholars trace its roots to the exile

look.title: Faithful without a Temple
look.text: Imagine your community's one holy building has burned, and you now live 500 miles away among people who speak another language. You cannot rebuild it. What could you still do, together, every week? What would you write down before the old people who remember it are gone?
look.prompt: List three things such a community could keep doing. Then match each one to something the lesson says the exiles did.

check.q: Why could the exiles not simply build a new Temple in Babylon?
choices: The law placed the Temple in Jerusalem, not elsewhere
check.why: The exiles had priests and skilled workers, but the Temple belonged in Jerusalem. They needed other ways to be faithful.

check.q: Which practice could the exiles keep in Babylon that marked who belonged?
check.why: The weekly day of rest, along with circumcision and food laws, could be kept anywhere. Sacrifice needed the Temple.

check.q: What does Ezekiel's vision of dry bones mean, according to the text?
choices: The house of Israel will live again and return
The Temple will never be rebuilt
The exiles should stay in Babylon
check.why: Ezekiel 37 says the bones are the whole house of Israel, and God will bring them into their land.

lessons.title: Cyrus and the Cylinder
lessons.mainIdea: In 539 BCE Persia's King Cyrus took Babylon, and both his clay cylinder and the book of Ezra describe him letting captive peoples go home.
reading: Babylon's power lasted less than a century. In 539 BCE the army of Cyrus, king of *Persia*, entered the city. Persia's empire would stretch from what is now Turkey to India, the largest the world had seen. Persian kings ruled through local governors and let subject peoples keep their gods, languages and laws, as long as they paid tribute and kept the peace.

The *Cyrus Cylinder*, found in Babylon in 1879, is Cyrus's announcement of his new rule. In it he says the god Marduk chose him. He says he took Babylon without a fight. He says he sent captive peoples, and the statues of their gods, back to their home shrines. Judah is not named. The cylinder states a general policy. It was written for Babylonians, in the style Babylonian kings had used before him.

The book of Ezra opens in the first year of Cyrus, 538 BCE. It quotes a *decree*, an official order. In it Cyrus says the God of heaven has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. He invites the exiles to go up and build it (Ezra 1:2-4). Ezra 6 quotes a second copy of the order, found in the royal archives. The text says Cyrus also returned the Temple's gold and silver vessels. Nebuchadnezzar had taken them.

The Bible's prophets treat Cyrus with wonder. Isaiah 45:1 calls him the LORD's anointed, the only non-Israelite given that title in the Bible. Historians note that the cylinder and Ezra fit together well, even though neither mentions the other. Cyrus had reasons of his own: loyal subjects near Egypt's border were useful. The text sees a different reason. Both can be described without deciding between them.

words.d: the empire based in today's Iran that took Babylon in 539 BCE and ruled Judah for two centuries
a clay record of King Cyrus's takeover of Babylon, found in 1879 and kept in the British Museum
an official order from a ruler

look.title: Cyrus announces his rule
look.text: Cyrus says that Marduk, the great lord, looked for a righteous ruler and chose him. He entered Babylon in peace, without battle. He gathered the peoples who had been brought to Babylon and returned them to their homes, and he sent the gods of their lands back to their own shrines.
look.cite: Cyrus Cylinder, Akkadian cuneiform, c. 539 BCE; British Museum, London (found 1879)
look.prompt: Cyrus credits Marduk; Ezra 1 credits the LORD. What might each writer want readers to believe about why Cyrus acted?

check.q: When did Cyrus take Babylon?
check.why: Cyrus entered Babylon in 539 BCE. Samaria fell in 722, Jerusalem in 586, and Alexander came in 332.

check.q: What does the Cyrus Cylinder say about Judah?
choices: It says the exiles must stay
It does not mention Judah at all
check.why: The cylinder describes a general policy of sending captive peoples home. Judah is never named on it.

check.q: What title does Isaiah 45:1 give Cyrus?
check.why: Isaiah calls Cyrus the LORD's anointed, the only non-Israelite given that title in the Bible.

lessons.title: A Smaller Temple
lessons.mainIdea: The returned exiles rebuilt the Temple by 515 BCE, a modest building that stood for the next five centuries.
reading: Not every exile went home. Many families had built lives in Babylon, and a Jewish community stayed there for over a thousand years. Those who returned found Jerusalem in ruins and its land held by others. Judah was now *Yehud*, a small province of the Persian empire, ruled by a governor. The first returns were led by Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, and the priest Jeshua.

Ezra 3 says the builders first set up the altar and then laid the Temple's foundation. Old people who remembered Solomon's Temple wept, while younger people shouted for joy. Then the work stopped. Neighbors, whom Ezra calls the enemies of Judah, offered to help and were refused. They then wrote to the Persian court to block the work. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah pushed the people to start again.

The Temple was finished in 515 BCE, in the sixth year of King Darius (Ezra 6:15). Historians call it the *Second Temple*, and the whole period from 515 BCE to 70 CE the Second Temple period. Haggai admits that next to the first one it looked like nothing (Haggai 2:3). There was no ark; the text never says what became of it. Yet this building, later enlarged by Herod, is the Temple of the Gospels.

The returnees also had to decide who belonged. Ezra and Nehemiah draw a sharp line around the people who came back from exile. Their books record lists of families and a painful dispute over marriages with local women. Readers have handled these chapters in different ways. Some see a small community protecting its identity; others see exclusion. Both note that the book of Ruth, about a Moabite woman who joins Israel, was read alongside them.

words.d: the Persian name for the small province of Judah after the exile
the Temple in Jerusalem finished in 515 BCE and destroyed by Rome in 70 CE
a region of an empire ruled by a governor who answers to the king

look.title: Weeping and shouting at once
look.text: Ezra 3:12-13 describes the day the foundation was laid. Old priests and elders who had seen the first Temple wept out loud. Many others shouted for joy. The text says the sound of weeping and the sound of joy could not be told apart, and the noise was heard far away.
look.prompt: Why might the same event make some people weep and others cheer? Describe a moment in your own community that could feel like this.

check.q: What was Yehud?
choices: The Persian province of Judah after the exile
The name of the Second Temple
check.why: Judah became the small Persian province of Yehud, ruled by a governor.

check.q: In what year was the Second Temple finished?
check.why: Ezra 6:15 places it in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BCE. Nehemiah's wall came in about 445 BCE.

check.q: How does the prophet Haggai describe the new Temple next to the old one?
check.why: Haggai 2:3 asks those who saw the first Temple whether the new one does not seem like nothing next to it.

lessons.title: Ezra Reads, Nehemiah Builds
lessons.mainIdea: Ezra brought the Torah to the people as a public reading, and Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's wall, both under Persian authority.
reading: Two leaders came from Persia in the 400s BCE. Ezra was a priest and a *scribe*, an expert in writing and in the law. The text says the Persian king sent him with a letter giving him authority to teach the law of his God (Ezra 7). Scholars debate the exact year of his arrival. Nehemiah was the king's cupbearer, a trusted servant. In about 445 BCE he asked King Artaxerxes for leave to rebuild Jerusalem's wall and was made governor.

Nehemiah's book reads like a memoir. He rides around the broken wall at night, then organizes families to each rebuild one section. Neighbors mock and threaten, so the builders work with weapons at their sides. The text says the wall was finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). A wall meant Jerusalem was a real city again, able to protect its people and its Temple.

The most important scene is in Nehemiah 8. On the first day of the seventh month, the people gather in a square, and Ezra reads the book of the law of Moses aloud from morning until noon. He stands on a wooden platform. Levites move through the crowd explaining the meaning. The people weep when they hear it, and the leaders tell them to eat, drink and rejoice instead. Then they keep the festival of Sukkot as the book describes.

Many scholars see this moment as a turning point. The people's guide is now a book, read in public and explained, not only a king or a priest. Jewish tradition honors Ezra as a second Moses who restored the Torah. The practice of reading the Torah aloud and explaining it, which continues in every synagogue today, has its first clear picture in this chapter.

words.d: an expert in writing and copying texts; Ezra is called a scribe skilled in the law of Moses
members of the tribe of Levi who served in the Temple and, in Nehemiah 8, explained the law to the people
the autumn festival of booths, when families live in temporary shelters for seven days

look.title: Reading with the meaning
look.text: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
look.prompt: The verse names three steps: reading clearly, giving the sense, causing understanding. Why is each step needed for a crowd hearing a book read aloud?

check.q: What was Nehemiah's job before he came to Jerusalem?
check.why: Nehemiah was a trusted servant, the king's cupbearer, and Artaxerxes made him governor of Judah.

check.q: According to Nehemiah 6:15, how long did the wall take to build?
check.why: The text says fifty-two days. Seven years is the time 1 Kings gives for Solomon's Temple.

check.q: What did Ezra do in the square in Nehemiah 8?
choices: Read the book of the law aloud while Levites explained it
Led the people back to Babylon
check.why: Ezra read from morning until noon on a wooden platform, and the Levites gave the sense.

lessons.title: Chronicles Tells It Again
lessons.mainIdea: First and Second Chronicles retell the story of Samuel and Kings for readers after the exile, with the Temple and David's line at the center.
reading: The Bible tells the story of the kings twice. Samuel and Kings tell it once. First and Second Chronicles tell it again, and many scholars think they were written after the exile, in the Persian period. The Hebrew name for the books means the events of the days. Reading the two versions side by side is one of the best ways to see how a writer shapes a story.

Chronicles begins with nine chapters of *genealogies*, lists of families reaching from Adam to the people who returned from exile. Then it tells David's story, but not all of it. The affair with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah and Absalom's revolt are left out. Instead David gathers materials and plans for the Temple. Solomon builds it. The northern kingdom of Israel almost drops from view; the writer follows Judah and the Temple.

Chronicles also adds. Second Chronicles 33 says the wicked King Manasseh repented in Babylon and was restored, a story Kings does not tell. Prayers, songs and priests fill the pages. The books end with the decree of Cyrus, the very words that open Ezra. In the Jewish order of the Bible, Chronicles is the last book of all, so the Tanakh ends with the call to go up to Jerusalem.

Why tell the story twice? The writer, whom scholars call the *Chronicler*, wrote for a small community with a Temple and no king. He gave them a past that pointed at their present: worship at the Temple, order in its music and priesthood, and hope in David's line. Christian Bibles place Chronicles right after Kings, as history. Jewish Bibles place it among the Writings, at the end. Both placements say something about how each tradition reads it.

words.d: lists of families and their descendants; 1 Chronicles opens with nine chapters of them
the scholars' name for the unknown writer of 1 and 2 Chronicles
the third part of the Jewish Bible, which includes Psalms, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles

look.title: Two tellings, by chapters
look.cite: Chapter counts in the King James Version (1611); the chapter divisions date from the 1200s CE
look.prompt: Add up the chapters in Samuel and Kings, then in Chronicles. What might the Chronicler have cut, and what did he add, to fit the story in fewer pages?

check.q: Which story does Chronicles leave out of David's life?
choices: His affair with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah
check.why: Chronicles skips the Bathsheba story and Absalom's revolt, and stresses David's Temple planning instead.

check.q: How does the Jewish Bible end?
choices: With Chronicles and the decree of Cyrus
With the fall of Jerusalem in 2 Kings
check.why: In the Jewish order, Chronicles is last, and it ends with Cyrus's call to go up to Jerusalem. Christian Bibles end the Old Testament with Malachi.

check.q: Why do many scholars think Chronicles was written for readers after the exile?
choices: It centers on the Temple and its worship, which mattered most to a community with no king
check.why: Chronicles is in Hebrew and is full of David. Its focus on Temple, priests and music fits the Persian-period community.

lessons.title: Esther at the Persian Court
lessons.mainIdea: The book of Esther tells how a Jewish queen in Persia risked her life to save her people, and gives Purim its story.
reading: Esther is set in *Susa*, a Persian royal city, under a king the text calls Ahasuerus. Many scholars identify him with Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BCE. The story opens with a banquet and a queen, Vashti, who refuses the king's order to appear. She is removed. A search for a new queen brings in Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai. On Mordecai's advice she keeps her people a secret.

The villain is Haman, the king's chief official. When Mordecai will not bow to him, Haman persuades the king to order the killing of all Jews in the empire on one day, chosen by lot. The word for lot is *pur*. Mordecai sends word to Esther. To approach the king uninvited could mean death. Mordecai asks who knows whether she came to the throne for such a time as this. Esther fasts, goes in, and over two banquets exposes Haman. He is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

The book is unusual in several ways. It never mentions God, prayer or the Temple. It is full of reversals: the day chosen for killing becomes a day of rescue. It is also the only book of the Hebrew Bible not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Some ancient readers questioned whether it belonged in scripture. A Greek version adds prayers and God's name; those additions are in the Apocrypha of Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

Esther is the story behind *Purim*, a spring holiday. Jewish communities read the whole book aloud from a scroll. They make noise at Haman's name. They give food to friends and gifts to the poor, and many wear costumes. Many readers see in the book a picture of life in a foreign empire. There is hidden identity, sudden danger, and survival through courage and wit.

words.d: a royal city of the Persian empire, in today's Iran, where the book of Esther is set
a lot, an object cast to make a choice; Haman casts one to pick a day, and Purim takes its name from it
the spring holiday when Jews read the book of Esther and celebrate the rescue it tells

look.title: Mordecai's message to Esther
look.text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
look.prompt: Mordecai never says God, yet many readers hear God behind the words from another place. What in the sentence supports that reading, and what leaves it open?

check.q: Where is the book of Esther set?
check.why: Esther's story unfolds at the Persian court in Susa. Daniel's stories are set in Babylon.

check.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
choices: It is the longest book in the Bible
check.why: The Hebrew Esther never names God, prays or mentions the Temple. The Greek version added prayers.

check.q: What holiday takes its name from the lot Haman cast?
check.why: Pur means lot, and Purim is the holiday of Esther. Hanukkah comes from the Maccabees' story.

lessons.title: Daniel in Babylon's Court
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel tells stories of Jewish young men staying faithful in a foreign court, and then visions of empires rising and falling.
reading: The book of Daniel is set in Babylon during the exile. Daniel and three friends, young men from Judah, are trained for the king's service. The first six chapters are *court tales*, stories about serving a foreign king without giving up one's faith. Daniel refuses the king's food and thrives on vegetables. He explains dreams that no Babylonian wise man can read. Later the writing on a wall spells out the fall of King Belshazzar.

Two stories are famous. In Daniel 3, the three friends refuse to bow to a golden statue and are thrown into a furnace. The text says they walk out unharmed. In Daniel 6, Daniel keeps praying toward Jerusalem against a royal ban and is thrown to the lions, and the text says he survives the night. In both, the men say they will obey God whether or not they are rescued.

Chapters 7 to 12 change form. They are *apocalyptic* visions. Beasts rise from the sea. A figure like a son of man comes with the clouds. Empires rise and fall in coded numbers. Part of the book, from 2:4 to 7:28, is written in *Aramaic* rather than Hebrew. The visions follow the history of the Persian and Greek empires closely, down to a king who attacks the Temple.

Readers date the book differently. Jewish and Christian tradition has read it as Daniel's own work from the 500s BCE. Many scholars think the visions were written or completed around 165 BCE, during the crisis under the Greek king Antiochus IV, to encourage people suffering then. Both readings agree on the book's message: empires pass, and faithfulness under pressure matters.

words.d: stories about a hero serving a foreign king, like Daniel 1-6 and the book of Esther
a kind of writing that reveals hidden things about history and its end through visions and symbols
a language close to Hebrew, used across the Persian empire; parts of Daniel and Ezra are written in it

look.title: Whether or not
look.text: If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
look.prompt: The three men say they will not bow even if not rescued. Why might the writer include the words But if not?

check.q: What kind of stories are Daniel 1 to 6?
choices: Court tales about serving a foreign king faithfully
check.why: Daniel and his friends serve Babylon's kings while keeping their faith. Esther is a court tale too.

check.q: What language is Daniel 2:4 to 7:28 written in?
check.why: That section is in Aramaic, the common language of the Persian empire. The rest of the book is Hebrew.

check.q: How do many scholars date the visions of Daniel 7 to 12?
choices: To the time of King David
To the exile in the 500s BCE
To the Roman period after Jesus
To about 165 BCE, under Antiochus IV
check.why: Many scholars place the visions in the Maccabean crisis, while tradition reads the book as Daniel's own work in the 500s BCE.

lessons.title: Alexander and the Greek World
lessons.mainIdea: Alexander's conquest in 332 BCE brought Greek language and culture to Judea, and the Torah was translated into Greek.
reading: Persian rule ended fast. Alexander the Great, king of Macedon, beat the Persian army and marched down the coast of Judea in 332 BCE. He died in Babylon nine years later, and his generals divided his empire. Judea was ruled first from Egypt, by the Ptolemies, and after 200 BCE from Syria, by the Seleucids. Greek became the language of trade, government and learning. Historians call this mix of Greek and local ways *Hellenism*.

Hellenism reached Jewish life everywhere. Cities got Greek names, theaters and gyms. Some Jews took Greek names and studied Greek philosophy. Others held tighter to Torah and worried about losing themselves. Both attitudes appear in the books written in these years. The tension between them helped bring on the revolt described in the next lesson.

The most lasting product of this period was a translation. In Alexandria, Egypt, the largest Jewish community outside Judea spoke Greek, not Hebrew. Beginning around 250 BCE, the Torah and then the other books were translated into Greek. This translation is called the *Septuagint*, from the Latin for seventy, after a legend that seventy-two scholars produced it.

The Septuagint mattered far beyond Egypt. It was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews, and later of the first Christians. Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow its wording. It also included books written in this period, such as the Maccabees, which is one reason Catholic and Orthodox Bibles contain books that the Hebrew Bible does not.

words.d: the spread of Greek language, ideas and customs across the lands Alexander conquered
the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Alexandria around 250 BCE
the Greek and Roman name for the land of Judah around Jerusalem

look.title: One province, five rulers
rows: Seleucid kings take Judea from the Ptolemies
look.cite: Standard dates; 1 Maccabees 1-4 for the revolt; Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, for Pompey and Herod
look.prompt: How many years passed between Cyrus and Herod? Which change of rulers do you think people in Jerusalem felt most, and why?

check.q: Who conquered Judea in 332 BCE?
check.why: Alexander took the region from Persia in 332 BCE. Pompey came for Rome in 63 BCE.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint, begun in Alexandria around 250 BCE, is the Greek Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and early Christians.

check.q: What does Hellenism mean?
choices: The worship of the god of Moab
The spread of Greek language and customs after Alexander
The rule of Rome over Judea
check.why: Hellenism is the mixing of Greek ways with local ones across Alexander's former empire.

lessons.title: The Maccabees and Hanukkah
lessons.mainIdea: A revolt against the Greek king Antiochus IV won back the Temple in 164 BCE, a story told in the books of Maccabees and remembered at Hanukkah.
reading: In 167 BCE the Seleucid king *Antiochus IV* banned the practice of Judaism. First Maccabees says he outlawed Sabbath and circumcision, burned Torah scrolls, and set up a foreign altar in the Temple. A priest named Mattathias refused to obey and fled to the hills with his five sons. His son Judah, nicknamed Maccabee, which may mean the hammer, led a guerrilla war against far larger armies.

In 164 BCE Judah's forces retook Jerusalem. They cleaned the Temple, built a new altar and *rededicated* it, that is, set it apart for worship again. First Maccabees 4 says they celebrated for eight days. The holiday of *Hanukkah*, which means dedication, remembers this. The story of a single day's oil burning for eight days is not in Maccabees. It appears later, in the Talmud (Shabbat 21b). Judah's family, the Hasmoneans, ruled Judea as priests and kings for about a century.

The story is told in 1 and 2 Maccabees, written in the 100s BCE, one in Hebrew and one in Greek. These books are part of the *Apocrypha*. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include them in the Old Testament and call them deuterocanonical. The Hebrew Bible does not include them, so most Protestant Bibles leave them out or print them in a separate section, as the King James Bible of 1611 did. Jewish tradition knows the story mainly through later writings.

Second Maccabees also tells of a mother and her seven sons who die rather than break the law. These are among the earliest stories of *martyrs*, people killed for their faith. The same book contains the earliest clear statement in Jewish writing of hope that the dead will rise. Both ideas became important to Jews and Christians in the centuries that followed.

words.d: the Seleucid Greek king who banned Jewish practice in 167 BCE and set off the Maccabean revolt
set apart for worship again; the Maccabees rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE
the eight-day winter holiday, meaning dedication, that remembers the Temple's rededication
books in the Greek Bible but not the Hebrew Bible; in Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments, not most Protestant ones
people killed for refusing to give up their faith

look.title: How many books in the Old Testament?
look.cite: Standard canon lists; the Hebrew Bible counts Samuel, Kings and the twelve minor prophets as one book each
look.prompt: The 24 and the 39 are the same words counted differently. Where do the extra books in the Catholic and Orthodox lists come from?

check.q: What did Antiochus IV do in 167 BCE, according to 1 Maccabees?
choices: Banned Jewish practice and set up a foreign altar in the Temple
check.why: 1 Maccabees says he outlawed Sabbath and circumcision and defiled the Temple, which set off the revolt.

check.q: Where does the story of the oil that burned for eight days come from?
choices: The Talmud, not the books of Maccabees
check.why: Maccabees describes an eight-day celebration but no oil miracle. The oil story appears in the Talmud, Shabbat 21b.

check.q: Which Bibles include 1 and 2 Maccabees in the Old Testament?
check.why: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles count them as deuterocanonical. The Hebrew Bible and most Protestant Bibles do not include them.

lessons.title: The World Jesus Was Born Into
lessons.mainIdea: By the first century Judea was under Rome and Herod, with a rebuilt Temple, synagogues, and several Jewish groups reading the same scriptures.
reading: The Hasmonean kingdom ended in 63 BCE, when the Roman general Pompey marched into Jerusalem. From then on Rome ruled, sometimes through local kings and sometimes through governors. In 37 BCE Rome made *Herod* king of Judea. He ruled until 4 BCE. He was a great builder and a feared ruler. Around 20 BCE he began enlarging the Second Temple into one of the largest sanctuaries in the Roman world. Its outer walls still stand in Jerusalem.

Jewish life in this period had several centers. The Temple in Jerusalem, with its priests and sacrifices, drew pilgrims at festivals. Synagogues in towns and villages gathered people for Torah reading and prayer every Sabbath. People spoke Aramaic at home, Greek in trade, and heard Hebrew in scripture. Jewish communities lived from Rome to Babylon.

Jews also disagreed about how to live by the Torah. The ancient historian Josephus describes several groups. The *Pharisees* taught in synagogues and valued oral traditions alongside the written law. The *Sadducees*, many of them priests, held to the written Torah and the Temple. The Essenes withdrew to live in strict communities; many scholars connect them to the Dead Sea Scrolls found near Qumran in 1947. Others hoped for a messiah who would end Roman rule.

This is the world of the Gospels. When the New Testament mentions Herod, the Temple, synagogues, Pharisees and Sadducees, it is describing this period. Jewish tradition traces rabbinic Judaism to the Pharisees. Christians trace their church to a Jewish teacher from Galilee in this same world. The Second Temple period ended in 70 CE, when Rome destroyed the Temple. Both traditions took shape in the years after.

words.d: the king Rome set over Judea from 37 to 4 BCE, who enlarged the Second Temple
a Jewish group that taught in synagogues and valued oral tradition alongside the written Torah
a Jewish group, many of them priests, tied to the Temple and the written Torah
ancient manuscripts found in caves near Qumran from 1947, including the oldest copies of biblical books

look.title: One Torah, several ways to live it
look.text: Around 30 CE, four Jews in Judea read the same Torah. A priest in Jerusalem sees the Temple as the center. A Pharisee in a Galilee village teaches on the Sabbath from oral traditions. A man at Qumran lives apart, copying scrolls. A farmer hopes for a king to send the Romans away. All four would say they keep the law of Moses.
look.prompt: Choose two of the four. What does each think matters most? How might they disagree, and what do they still share?

check.q: Who began enlarging the Second Temple around 20 BCE?
check.why: Herod, king under Rome from 37 to 4 BCE, rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale. Zerubbabel led the first rebuilding in the 500s BCE.

check.q: Which group valued oral traditions alongside the written Torah and taught in synagogues?
check.why: Josephus describes the Pharisees this way. The Sadducees held to the written Torah and the Temple.

check.q: When did the Second Temple period end?
choices: In 70 CE, when Rome destroyed the Temple
In 164 BCE, when the Maccabees won
In 515 BCE, when the Temple was finished
check.why: The Second Temple stood from 515 BCE until Rome destroyed it in 70 CE.

review.q: Which two years mark Babylon's deportations from Judah?
review.why: Jehoiachin was taken in 597 BCE and the Temple burned in 586 BCE. The other pairs belong to Assyria, Persia and the Maccabees.

choices: A scroll of the book of Ezra
A clay record of Cyrus's takeover of Babylon
A map of the return to Jerusalem
review.why: The cylinder, found in 1879, is Cyrus's announcement in cuneiform. It does not mention Judah.

choices: Ezra read the Torah aloud to the people
review.why: Ezra read the law from a platform while Levites explained it. The wall's finish is in Nehemiah 6.

review.q: How does Chronicles differ from Samuel and Kings?
choices: It leaves out David's sins and focuses on the Temple and Judah
It tells the story of the judges
It ends with the fall of Jerusalem
review.why: Chronicles skips Bathsheba and Absalom, follows Judah, and ends with Cyrus's decree.

review.q: Which two books are court tales about Jews serving a foreign king?
review.why: Esther is set in Persia's court and Daniel 1-6 in Babylon's. Ezra and Nehemiah are about the return.

choices: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
review.why: The Septuagint was translated in Alexandria from about 250 BCE and was used by Greek-speaking Jews and early Christians.

review.q: Why do Catholic Bibles include 1 and 2 Maccabees while the Hebrew Bible does not?
choices: Because Jews do not celebrate Hanukkah
Because the books were lost until 1947
Because they were written after Jesus
Because they were in the Greek Bible but not the Hebrew canon
review.why: The Maccabees are in the Septuagint. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles kept them; the Hebrew canon and most Protestant Bibles did not.

review.q: Which sentence about the world of the Gospels is correct?
choices: Judea was under Rome, and Pharisees and Sadducees disagreed about the Torah
Judea was still ruled by Persia
The Temple had not yet been rebuilt
review.why: By the first century Rome ruled, Herod had enlarged the Temple, and Josephus describes several groups with different views.
